In [[mathematics]], a '''uniformly bounded representation'''  <math>T</math> of a [[locally compact group]] <math>G</math> on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H</math> is a [[homomorphism]] into the bounded invertible operators which is continuous for the [[strong operator topology]], and such that <math>\sup_{g\in G} \|T_g\|_{B(H)}</math> is finite. In 1947 [[Béla Szőkefalvi-Nagy]] established that any uniformly bounded representation of the integers or the real numbers is '''unitarizable''', i.e. conjugate by an invertible operator to a [[unitary representation]]. For the integers this gives a criterion for an invertible operator to be similar to a [[unitary operator]]: the [[operator norm]]s of all the positive and negative powers must be uniformly bounded. The result on unitarizability of uniformly bounded representations was extended in 1950 by [[Jacques Dixmier|Dixmier]], Day and Nakamura-Takeda to all locally compact [[amenable group]]s, following essentially the method of proof of Sz-Nagy. The result is known to fail for non-amenable groups such as [[SL(2,R)|SL(2,'''R''')]] and the [[free group]] on two generators. {{harvtxt|Dixmier|1950}} conjectured that a locally compact group is amenable [[if and only if]] every uniformly bounded representation is unitarizable.

==Statement==
Let ''G'' be a locally compact [[amenable group]] and let ''T''<sub>''g''</sub> be a homomorphism of ''G'' into ''GL''(''H''), the group of an invertible operators on a Hilbert space such that

*for every ''x'' in ''H'' the vector-valued ''gx'' on ''G'' is continuous;
*the operator norms of the operators ''T''<sub>''g''</sub> are uniformly bounded.

Then there is a positive invertible operator ''S'' on ''H'' such that ''S'' ''T''<sub>''g''</sub> ''S''<sup>−1</sup> is unitary for every ''g'' in ''G''.

As a consequence, if ''T'' is an invertible operator with all its positive and negative powers uniformly bounded in operator norm, then ''T'' is conjugate by a positive invertible operator to a unitary.

==Proof==
By assumption the continuous functions

:<math>\displaystyle{f_{x,y}(g)=(T_g^{-1}x,T_g^{-1}y),}</math>

generate a separable unital C* subalgebra ''A'' of the uniformly bounded continuous functions on ''G''. By construction the algebra is invariant under left translation. By amenability there is an invariant state φ on ''A''. It follows that

:<math>\displaystyle{(x,y)_0 =\varphi(f_{x,y})}</math>

is a new inner product on ''H'' satisfying

:<math>\displaystyle{M^{-1}\|x\| \le \|x\|_0 \le M\|x\|}</math>

where

:<math>\displaystyle{M=\sup_g \|T_g\| < \infty.}</math>

So there is a positive invertible operator ''P'' such that

:<math>\displaystyle{(x,y)_0 =(Px,y).}</math>

By construction

:<math>\displaystyle{(T_gx,T_gy)_0=(x,y)_0.}</math>

Let ''S'' be the unique positive square root of ''P''. Then

:<math>\displaystyle{(ST_g x,ST_gy)=(PT_gx,T_gy)=(Px,y) =(Sx,Sy).}</math>

Applying ''S''<sup>−1</sup> to ''x'' and ''y'', it follows that

:<math>\displaystyle{(ST_gS^{-1} x, ST_gS^{-1} y)=(x,y).}</math>

Since the operators

:<math>\displaystyle{U_g=ST_gS^{-1}}</math>
 
are invertible, it follows that they are unitary.

==Examples of non-unitarizable representations==

===SL(2,R)===
The [[complementary series representation|complementary series]] of irreducible unitary representations of SL(2,R) was introduced by {{harvtxt|Bargmann|1947}}. These representations can be realized on functions on the circle or on the [[Number line|real line]]: the [[Cayley transform]] provides the unitary equivalence between the two realizations.<ref>{{harvnb|Sugiura|1990|pp=391–393}}</ref>

In fact for 0 < σ < 1/2 and ''f'', ''g'' continuous functions on the circle define

:<math>\displaystyle{(f,g)_\sigma={1\over 4\pi^2} \int_{-\pi}^\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(s)\overline{g(t)} k_\sigma(s-t) \,ds\, dt,}</math>

where

:<math>\displaystyle{k_\sigma(s)=(1-\cos s)^{\sigma-1/2}.}</math>

Since the function ''k''<sub>σ</sub> is integrable, this integral converges. In fact

:<math>\displaystyle{(f,g)_\sigma \le \|f\|\cdot \|g\|,}</math>

where the norms are the usual L<sup>2</sup> norms.

The functions

:<math>\displaystyle{f_m(t)=e^{imt}}</math>

are orthogonal with

:<math>\displaystyle{(f_m,f_m)_\sigma=\prod_{i=1}^{|m|} {i-1/2-\sigma\over i-1/2+\sigma}= {\Gamma(1/2 +\sigma)\Gamma(|m|+1/2-\sigma)\over \Gamma(1/2-\sigma)\Gamma(m+1/2+\sigma)}.}</math>

Since these quantities are positive, (''f'',''g'')<sub>σ</sub> defines an inner product. The Hilbert space completion is denoted by ''H''<sub>σ</sub>.

For ''F'', ''G'' continuous functions of compact support on '''R''', define

:<math>\displaystyle{(F,G)_\sigma^\prime=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\int_{-\infty}^\infty F(x)\overline{G(y)} |x-y|^{2\sigma-1}\,dx\, dy.}</math>

Since, regarded as distributions, the [[Fourier transform]] of |''x''|<sup>2σ – 1</sup> is C<sub>σ</sub>|''t''|<sup>−2σ</sup> for some positive constant C<sub>σ</sub>, the above expression can be rewritten:

:<math>\displaystyle{(F,G)_\sigma^\prime=C_\sigma\int_{-\infty}^\infty \widehat{F}(t)\overline{\widehat{G}(t)} |t|^{-2\sigma}\, dt.}</math>

Hence it is an inner product. Let ''H'''<sub>σ</sub> denote its Hilbert space completion.
 
The Cayley transform gives rise to an operator ''U'':

:<math>\displaystyle{Uf(x)=2^{\sigma/2 - 3/4} \pi^{-1} |x+i|^{1-2\sigma} f\left({x-i\over x+i}\right).}</math>

''U'' extends to an isometry of ''H''<sub>σ</sub> onto ''H'' '<sub>σ</sub>. Its adjoint is given by

:<math>\displaystyle{U^*F(e^{it})=2^{3/4-\sigma/2} \pi |1- e^{it}|^{1-2\sigma} F\left({1+e^{it}\over 1-e^{it}}\right).}</math>

The Cayley transform exchanges the actions by [[Möbius transformation]]s of SU(1,1) on '''S'''<sup>1</sup> and of SL(2, '''R''') on '''R'''.

The operator ''U'' intertwines corresponding actions of SU(1,1) on ''H''<sub>σ</sub> and SL(2,'''R''') on ''H'' '<sub>σ</sub>.

For ''g'' in SU(1,1) given by

:<math>\displaystyle{g=\begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ \overline{\beta} & \overline{\alpha}\end{pmatrix},}</math>

with

:<math>\displaystyle{|\alpha|^2 - |\beta|^2=1,}</math>

and ''f'' continuous, set

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi_\sigma(g^{-1}) f(z)=|\overline{\beta}z+\overline{\alpha}|^{1-2\sigma}f\left({\alpha z +\beta\over\overline{\beta}z +\overline{\alpha}}\right).}</math>

For ''g''' in SL(2,'''R''') given by

:<math>\displaystyle{g^\prime=\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix},}</math>

with ''ad'' – ''bc'' = 1, set

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi^\prime_\sigma((g^\prime)^{-1}) F(x) =|cx+d|^{1-2\sigma} F\left({ax+b\over cx +d}\right).}</math>

If ''g'' ' corresponds to ''g'' under the Cayley transform then

:<math>\displaystyle{U\pi_\sigma(g)U^* =\pi^\prime_\sigma(g^\prime).}</math>

Polar decomposition shows that SL(2,R) = ''KAK'' with ''K'' = SO(2) and ''A'' the subgroup of positive diagonal matrices. ''K'' corresponds to the diagonal matrices in SU(1,1). Since evidently ''K'' acts unitarily on ''H''<sub>σ</sub> and ''A'' acts unitarily on ''H'' '<sub>σ</sub>, both representations are unitary. The representations are irreducible because the action of the Lie algebra on the basis vectors ''f''<sub>m</sub> is irreducible. This family of irreducible unitary representations is called the '''complementary series'''.

{{harvtxt|Ehrenpreis|Mautner|1955}} constructed an analytic continuation of this family of representations as follows.<ref>{{harvnb|Lohoué|1980}}</ref> If ''s'' = σ + iτ, g lies in SU(1,1) and ''f'' in ''H''<sub>σ</sub>, define

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi_s(g^{-1}) f(z)=|\overline{\beta}z+\overline{\alpha}|^{1-2s}f\left({\alpha z +\beta\over\overline{\beta}z +\overline{\alpha}}\right).}</math>

Similarly if ''g'' ' lies in SL(2,'''R''') and ''F'' in  ''H'' '<sub>σ</sub>, define

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi^\prime_s((g^\prime)^{-1}) F(x) =|cx+d|^{1-2s} F\left({ax+b\over cx +d}\right).}</math>

As before the unitary ''U'' intertwines these two actions. ''K'' acts unitarily on ''H''<sub>σ</sub> and ''A'' by a uniformly bounded representation on ''H'' '<sub>σ</sub>. The action of the standard basis of the complexification Lie algebra on this basis can be computed:<ref>{{harvnb|Bargmann|1947|p=613}}</ref>

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi_s(L_0)f_m=mf_m, \,\, \pi_s(L_{-1})f_m=-(m+1/2+s)f_{m+1},\,\, \pi_s(L_1)f_m=-(m-1/2-s)f_{m-1}.}</math>

If the representation were unitarizable for τ ≠ 0, then the similarity operator ''T'' on ''H''<sub>σ</sub> would have to commute with ''K'', since ''K'' preserves the original inner product. The vectors ''Tf''<sub>''m''</sub> would therefore still be orthogonal for the new inner product and  
the operators

:<math>\displaystyle{L_i^\prime=TL_iT^{-1}}</math>

would satisfy the same relations for

:<math>\displaystyle{f_m^\prime = Tf_m=\lambda_m f_m.}</math>

In this case

:<math> \displaystyle{[L_m^\prime,L_n^\prime]=(m-n)L_{m+n}^\prime,\,\,(L_i^\prime)^*=L_{-i}^\prime.}</math>

It is elementary to verify that infinitesimally such a representation cannot exist if τ ≠ 0.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Bargmann|1947}}
*{{harvnb|Howe|Tan|1992}}
*{{harvnb|Lang|1985|pp=122–123}}</ref>

Indeed, let ''v''<sub>0</sub> = ''f'' '<sub>0</sub> and set

:<math>\displaystyle{v_1=L^\prime_{-1}v_0.}</math>

Then

:<math>\displaystyle{L^\prime_1 v_1=c v_{0}}</math>

for some constant ''c''. On the other hand,

:<math>\displaystyle{\|v_{1}\|^2=(L_{-1}^\prime v_0,v_{1})=(v_0,L_1^\prime v_{1})=\overline{c}\|v_0\|^2.}</math>

Thus ''c'' must be real and positive. The formulas above show that

:<math>\displaystyle{c={1\over 4}-s^2={1\over 4}-\sigma^2 +\tau^2 -2i\sigma\tau,}</math>

so the representation π<sub>''s''</sub> is unitarizable only if τ = 0.

===Free group on two generators===
The group ''G'' = SL(2,'''R''') contains the discrete group Γ = SL(2,'''Z''') as a closed subgroup of finite covolume, since this subgroup acts on the upper half plane with a fundamental domain of finite hyperbolic area.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Serre|1977}}
*{{harvnb|Gelfand|Graev|Pyatetskii-Shapiro|1969}}</ref> The group SL(2,'''Z''') contains a subgroup of index 12 isomorphic to '''F'''<sub>2</sub> the free group on two generators.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Magnus|Karrass|Solitar|1976}}
*{{harvnb|Serre|1980}}</ref> Hence ''G'' has a subgroup Γ<sub>1</sub> of finite covolume, isomorphic to '''F'''<sub>2</sub>. If ''L'' is a closed subgroup of finite covolume in a locally compact group ''G'', and π is non-unitarizable uniformly bounded representation of ''G'' on a Hilbert space ''L'', then its restriction to ''L'' is uniformly bounded and non-unitarizable. For if not, applying a bounded invertible operator, the inner product can be made invariant under ''L''; and then in turn invariant under ''G'' by redefining

:<math>\displaystyle{(x,y)_1=\int_{H\backslash G} (gx,gy) \, dg.}</math>

As in the previous proof, uniform boundedess guarantees that the norm defined by this inner product is
equivalent to the original inner product. But then the original representation would be unitarizable on ''G'', a contradiction. The same argument works for any discrete subgroup of ''G'' of finite covolume. In particular the [[surface group]]s, which are cocompact subgroups, have uniformly bounded representations that are not unitarizable.

There are more direct constructions of uniformly bounded representations of free groups that are non-unitarizable: these are surveyed in {{harvtxt|Pisier|2001}}. The first such examples are described in 
{{harvtxt|Figà-Talamanca|Picardello|1983}}, where an analogue of the complementary series is constructed.

Later {{harvtxt|Szwarc|1988}} gave a related but simpler construction, on the Hilbert space ''H'' = <math>\ell</math><sup>2</sup>('''F'''<sub>2</sub>), of a holomorphic family of uniformly bounded representations π<sub>''z''</sub> of '''F'''<sub>2</sub> for  |z| < 1; these are non-unitarizable when  1/√3 < |''z''| < 1 and ''z'' is not real. Let ''L''(''g'') denote the reduced word length on '''F'''<sub>2</sub> for a given set of generators ''a'', ''b''. Let ''T'' be the bounded operator defined on basis elements by

:<math>\displaystyle{Te_1=0,\,\, Te_g=e_{g^\prime},}</math>

where ''g'' ' is obtained by erasing the last letter in the expression of ''g'' as a reduced word; identifying ''F''<sub>2</sub> with the vertices of its [[Cayley graph]], a rooted tree,{{sfn|Serre|1980}} this corresponds to passing from a vertex to the next closest vertex to the origin or root. For |z| < 1

:<math>\displaystyle{\pi_z(g) = (I-zT)^{-1}\lambda(g)(I-zT)}</math>

is well-defined on finitely supported functions. {{harvtxt|Pytlik|Szwarc|1986}} had earlier proved that it extends to a uniformly bounded representation on ''H'' satisfying

:<math>\displaystyle{\|\pi_z(g)\|\le {1+|z|\over 1-|z|}.}</math>

In fact it is easy to check that the operator 
λ(''g'')''T''λ(''g'')<sup>−1</sup> – ''T'' has finite rank, with range''V''<sub>''g''</sub>, the finite-dimensional space of functions supported on the set of vertices joining ''g'' to the origin. For on any function vanishing on this finite set, ''T'' and λ(''g'')''T''λ(''g'')<sup>−1</sup> are equal; and they both leave invariant ''V''<sub>''g''</sub>, on which they acts as contractions and adjoints of each other. Hence if ''f'' has finite support and norm 1,

:<math>\displaystyle{\|\pi_z(g)f\|=\|\lambda(g)f+\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{n+1} T^n[T,\lambda(g)]f\|\le 1 + 2 \sum_{n=0}^n |z|^{n+1} ={1+|z|\over 1-|z|}.}</math>

For |z| < 1/√3, these representations are all similar to the regular representation λ. If on the other hand 1/√3 < |z| <1, then the operator

:<math>\displaystyle{D=\pi_z(a)+\pi_z(a^{-1}) + \pi_z(b) +\pi_z(b^{-1})}</math>

satisfies

:<math> \displaystyle{Df=(3z +z^{-1})f}</math>

where ''f'' in ''H'' is defined by

:<math>\displaystyle{f(1)=1,\,\, f(g)={3\over 4} (3z)^{-L(g)} \,\,(g\ne 1).}</math>

Thus, if ''z'' is not real, ''D'' has an eigenvalue which is not real. But then π<sub>''z''</sub> cannot be unitarizable, since otherwise ''D'' would be similar to a self-adjoint operator.

==Dixmier problem==
[[Jacques Dixmier]] asked in 1950 whether amenable groups are characterized by '''unitarizability''', i.e. the property that all their uniformly bounded representations are unitarizable.  This problem remains open to this day.

An elementary [[induced representation|induction]] argument shows that a subgroup of a unitarizable group remains unitarizable.  Therefore, the [[von Neumann conjecture]] would have implied a positive answer to Dixmier's problem, had it been true.  In any case, it follows that a counter-example to Dixmier's conjecture could only be a non-amenable group without free subgroups. In particular, Dixmier's conjecture is true for all [[linear group]]s by the [[Tits alternative]].

A criterion due to Epstein and [[Nicolas Monod|Monod]] shows that there are also non-unitarizable groups without free subgroups.<ref>{{harvnb|Epstein|Monod|2009}}</ref> In fact, even some [[Burnside group]]s are non-unitarizable, as shown by Monod and Ozawa.<ref>{{harvnb|Monod|Ozawa|2010}}</ref>

Considerable progress has been made by [[Gilles Pisier|Pisier]] who linked unitarizability to a notion of factorization length. This allowed him to solve a modified form of the Dixmier problem.

The potential gap between unitarizability and amenability can be further illustrated by the following open problems, all of which become elementary if "unitarizable" were replaced by "amenable":

*Is the [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of two unitarizable groups unitarizable?
*Is a directed union of unitarizable groups unitarizable?
*If <math>G</math> contains a normal amenable subgroup <math>N</math> such <math>G/N</math> is unitarizable, does it follow that <math>G</math> is unitarizable? (It is elementary that <math>G</math> is unitarizable if <math>N</math> is so and <math>G/N</math> is amenable.)
